Based on chapter 11 of Gelman et al., Bayesian Workflow.

  • About 1 minute
  • Morning, everyone. Today is chapter 11 of Bayesian Workflow, and the question underneath it is a practical one: when can we actually trust the draws our sampler hands us?
  • Point at the purple bandLet me make you a promise up front. By the end you’ll know what a single chain can’t tell you, what R-hat, ESS and MCSE each test, and how many digits you’re allowed to report.
  • Point at the routeHere’s how we’ll get there. First, where samples actually live, which isn’t where most of us picture them. Then how the sampler gets there: warm-up, and why one chain isn’t enough. Then the three checks. And we’ll finish on what this means for the tool we build.
  • It’s about 22 minutes, and I’ll keep time for questions at the end. Let’s start with a picture.

    The most likely point is not where your samples land

    Mass = density × volume. Density peaks at the mode, but there is far more volume further out, so almost all the mass sits well away from the mode.

    FTN
    mass(r)  ∝  exp⁡(−r2/2)⏟density⋅rD−1⏟volume\text{mass}(r) \;\propto\; \underbrace{\exp(-r^2/2)}_{\text{density}} \cdot \underbrace{r^{D-1}}_{\text{volume}}mass(r)∝densityexp(−r2/2)​​⋅volumerD−1​​

    The volume of the thin shell at distance r grows like rD−1, so the mass peaks at r ≈ √D.

  • About 2½ minutes · keys 1–9 and 0 set D
  • D = 1Here are 2,000 draws from a standard normal, the most ordinary bell curve there is. In one dimension they sit on a line, and the most likely point, the mode, is right in the thick of them. Almost every draw is within 2 of it. That’s the picture most of us carry around.
  • Drag to 2Give each draw a second coordinate and we get a disc. Still crowded round the middle, but fewer inside the circle.
  • Drag to 3A third coordinate, and it’s a ball. Look at the count on the right: already a quarter of the draws sit outside the radius-2 ball.
  • Drag to 10Now, I’d love to show you ten dimensions… but my brain is on the three-dimensional plan. (Click Upgrade for the laugh, then carry on.) So I won’t pretend to draw it. The numbers on the right are still exact, and that’s where to look.
  • Pause before 100A question for you. A hierarchical MMM easily has a hundred parameters or more. In a hundred dimensions, how many of these 2,000 draws land within 2 of the mode? Have a guess.
  • Drag to 100None. Zero out of 2,000. The typical draw is about 10 away. The most likely point is not where your samples land.
  • ClickWhy? Mass is density times volume. Density is highest at the mode; nobody argues with that. But take all the points at distance r from the mode: together they form a thin shell, and the volume of that shell grows like r to the power D − 1. Right at the mode there’s plenty of density but almost no volume. Far out there’s enormous volume but almost no density. The mass ends up where the two balance, at a distance of about the square root of D. In a hundred dimensions, that’s 10.
  • So where exactly does it end up?
  • If asked“What exactly is the typical set?” It’s the region that holds almost all the probability: the points whose log density is close to the average log density of a draw, not to the maximum. Formally, it’s every point whose −log p is within a small tolerance of the entropy, the expected value of −log p. As the dimension grows it captures nearly all the probability, and for a standard normal it’s the thin shell at a distance of about √D from the mode. The mode itself isn’t in it.

    The region where nearly all the probability mass lives. It’s the points whose log density is close to its average, not its maximum.

  • About 1½ minutes
  • This is that same idea as a 3D sketch. It’s not to scale; the real numbers are in the table.
  • Point at the calloutsHighest density in the middle. Almost all the mass out here, in a thin shell. That shell has a name: the typical set.
  • If that feels abstract, think of coin flips. Flip a 60/40 coin a hundred times. The single most likely sequence is all heads. Has anyone ever seen it? No. What you actually get is about sixty heads in some order. Each of those sequences is less likely than all heads, but there are so many of them that together they hold nearly all the probability. All heads is the mode; the sixty-ish sequences are the typical set.
  • Our posteriors work the same way. The single best parameter combination isn’t representative of the posterior at all.
  • Point at the tableAnd it gets more extreme as the dimension grows: in a hundred dimensions essentially nothing is within 2 of the mode, and the shell stays thin while it moves further out.
  • So what does that mean for the algorithms we use to fit our models?
    • Bayesian Workflow · Chapter 114

    Optimisers find the peak; samplers find the mass

    Optimisergradient ascent on log density, as MAP / L-BFGS

    HMCNUTS, every position kept

    One point · not typical · no uncertainty

  • About 2 minutes · P plays
  • Press PlayTwo algorithms, same start, same hundred-dimensional posterior. The top pictures are 3D sketches; the chart underneath is the real distance from the mode.
  • Watch red first. That’s an optimiser, the thing behind a MAP estimate. It follows the slope like a heat-seeking missile and lands on the mode. Notice it went straight through the shell on the way, through all the probability mass, and kept going.
  • Now purple. That’s HMC. It also follows the slope at first, but it carries momentum, a bit like a satellite. When it reaches the shell it keeps travelling around it instead of falling to the bottom.
  • Point at the chartSame story in one line: red ends at zero, purple lives in the band.
  • So any tool that hands you a MAP estimate is handing you the red dot: the single best point, not a typical one, with no uncertainty attached.
  • HMC doesn’t get there for free, though. It needs tuning first, and that’s warm-up.
    • Bayesian Workflow · Chapter 115

    Warm-up tunes two knobs, then throws its draws away

    1. I · Find the typical set1–75

      The puck falls from the start into the bulk of the posterior. Only the step size ε adapts, aiming for about 80% acceptance.

    2. II · Learn the scales76–250

      Windows of 25, 50 and 100 draws measure each parameter’s spread. After each window (◆) the mass matrix updates and ε is re-tuned.

    3. III · Settle the step size251–300

      Mass matrix fixed. A last round of ε tuning; its average becomes the step size for sampling.

    4. Sampling301–600

      Both knobs frozen. These draws are kept; every warm-up draw is thrown away.

  • About 1½ minutes · P plays and pauses
  • Before a single draw is kept, Stan tunes two knobs that nobody in this room ever sets: the step size, and the mass matrix, which rescales each parameter. Picture a frictionless bowl whose height is the negative log of the posterior, so the most probable point is the bottom. Each iteration we flick a puck in a random direction and let it glide for a while, and the next draw is picked from somewhere along that path.
  • Press PlayStage one: find the typical set. We start far out, like a real model does, and fall in within a few iterations. Only the step size is adapting.
  • Point at the thin linesThose thin lines with dots are the puck’s actual paths, one per iteration; each dot is one small step of the simulation. They look different every time for three reasons. First, every iteration starts with a fresh random flick, a new direction and a new strength, so the puck glides somewhere new. Second, the length isn’t fixed: the sampler keeps extending the path until it starts to turn back on itself, so some paths are short and some are long. And third, the next draw is picked from somewhere along the path, not necessarily the end, so the next path starts from wherever that was.
  • Stage two: learn the scales. In windows of 25, 50 and 100 iterations, Stan measures how spread out each parameter is. Each diamond on the bar is an update. Watch the paths after each diamond: the steps stretch sideways, because the mass matrix now knows the posterior is about ten times wider across than up, so each step covers more ground in the wide direction.
  • When it pausesStage three settles the step size. And then all of this, everything grey, is thrown away. A few divergences in here are normal; only the ones during sampling count.
  • Play samplingNow the knobs are frozen and every draw is kept. In an MMM our parameters always live on very different scales, and the mass matrix is what lets one step size suit them all.
  • So now we have a well-tuned chain. Can we trust it?
  • If asked“Why are the early paths so short and choppy?” Before the mass matrix has learned the scales, one step size has to suit the narrowest direction, which here is ten times narrower than the widest. So the puck takes lots of small steps and zig-zags. Once the mass matrix rescales the space, the same number of steps covers far more ground.
  • If asked“Why do the dots get further apart or closer together?” That’s the step size changing. During warm-up Stan keeps nudging it up or down to hit about 80% acceptance, and it restarts after each mass-matrix update. In sampling it’s fixed.
  • If asked“Is this a real run?” Yes: a real NUTS run with Stan-style warm-up on a 2-D normal with standard deviations 10 and 1.
  • If asked“Does the mass matrix handle correlations?” Not by default. Stan’s default is diagonal: it fixes different scales, not correlations. Strong correlations need a dense metric or a reparameterisation.
    • Bayesian Workflow · Chapter 116

    One chain can lie to you

    A chain can only report on the territory it has visited.

    fallwarm-upkept draws

    What if we start several chains in different places, and compare them?

    ParameterMeanSD2.5%97.5%Bulk-ESSTail-ESSR-hatDivergences
    x₁ · this chain
    x₁ · truth
  • About 2½ minutes · the centrepiece
  • Plays on entryHere’s one chain on a hundred-dimensional posterior. It falls in, warms up and samples. The trace plot is textbook. R-hat 1.00, over a thousand effective draws, no divergences.
  • Honest question: if this landed on your desk, would you sign it off? (Pause.) I would.
  • ClickNow let’s zoom out. Same landscape, same axis. There’s a second island, exactly like the first, holding half the probability, and the chain never went there. Every diagnostic stayed green. The interval it reports is four times too narrow, and its mean is six of its own standard deviations from the truth.
  • Why did nothing complain? Split-R-hat on one chain compares its first half with its second half, and both halves sit on the same island, so they agree. ESS only measures how well the chain mixes where it is, and it mixes beautifully on that island. And each island on its own is a friendly bell shape, so there are no divergences. Those checks test whether a chain is stable. None of them can tell you whether it’s complete.
  • In real models this shows up as label switching, weak identification, or, in our MMMs, collinear channels and saturation curves that can explain the same sales two ways. Usually it’s ridges rather than clean islands, but the lesson holds: a single chain can be confidently incomplete.
  • ClickAnd the fix isn’t a longer chain. A million more iterations would stay on the same island. The fix is more chains, started in different places. Which is where we go next.
  • If asked“They’re only 12 apart. Why doesn’t it cross?” Halfway between them the density is tens of millions of times lower than at a peak. To climb over, the chain would need a wildly unusual push in exactly that direction, so in practice it never does.
  • If asked“Didn’t you pick the start?” Yes, for the demo. From a random start it lands on either island about half the time, and you can’t tell which half you’re in from the chain alone.
  • If asked“What am I looking at on the map?” The first two coordinates seen from above. The other 98 look the same on both islands.
  • If asked“Is this a real run?” Yes: a real NUTS run with Stan-default warm-up on a 50/50 mixture of two 100-dimensional normals, peaks 12 apart.
    • Bayesian Workflow · Chapter 117

    One chain can show it’s stable, not that it’s complete

    AIslands

    BHasn’t forgotten its start

    CA corner it can’t reach

    DOne chain stuck

    One chain sees it?Several chains see it?
    A✗ No every diagnostic green✓ Yes different levels
    B~ Partly split-R-hat flags the drift✓ Yes haven’t met

    • Cheap: chains run in parallel; four ≈ one.
    • Better numbers: R-hat and ESS improve.
    • Longer isn’t a fix: it sees one neighbourhood.
  • About 2 minutes
  • Slide 6 wasn’t a one-off. Here are four ways a single chain misleads you, all from real runs. On its own, each of these could pass, or at best raise a vague doubt.
  • A, you’ve already seen: the islands. B hasn’t forgotten where it started; it’s still drifting. C can’t get into a narrow corner, and a few divergences are the only hint. And D keeps stalling, yet its summary numbers still look reasonable.
  • ClickNow add three more chains started elsewhere, and every one of these jumps out. In A they sit at different levels. In B they haven’t met. In C they disagree on depth. In D one chain is plainly unlike the rest.
  • That’s the whole idea in one line: checks within a chain tell you it’s stable; comparing chains tells you whether it’s complete. On the next slide, R-hat turns that comparison into a number.
  • If asked“Can’t I just look at the trace more carefully?” For B and D, sometimes. For A, no: that single trace is genuinely perfect. And nobody inspects trace plots for hundreds of parameters; R-hat does the comparison for every parameter at once.
  • If asked“Isn’t C what divergences are for?” Yes, and they’re a valuable warning. But a chain that never gets near the neck produces few or none, and only the other chains show what it missed.
  • If asked“Why do C and D matter for MMM?” Hierarchical MMMs, with markets or brands sharing a prior, have exactly this funnel shape when the group-level spread is small. The usual fix is the non-centred parameterisation.
  • If asked“How were these run?” All real NUTS runs with Stan-default warm-up. A is slide 6’s mixture. B is a 2-D normal with correlation 0.9995, short warm-up and tree depth capped at 3. C and D are eight schools, centred. In D the stuck chain left warm-up with a step size about 30 times smaller than the others. Seeds were picked to show each failure, but they aren’t rare: 6 of 34 eight-schools seeds had a chain like D’s.

    How many chains to catch the islands reliably?

    Chains1248
    All on one island (hidden)100%50%12.5%< 1%
    FTN
    R^≈spread across all chainsspread within chains\hat{R} \approx \sqrt{\dfrac{\text{spread across all chains}}{\text{spread within chains}}}R^≈spread within chainsspread across all chains​​

    Rank-normalised split-R-hat (Vehtari et al., 2021): each chain is split in half, and it is computed on ranks.

  • About 3 minutes · four clicks
  • R-hat makes that comparison automatic. It compares the spread inside each chain with the spread of all the chains pooled together. If the chains agree, those two are the same, and R-hat is 1.
  • Click through 0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3Watch how little separation it takes. At a third of a standard deviation it’s already flagged. That sensitivity is the point. Two extra tricks are built in: each chain is split in half, so a single drifting chain gets caught too, and it works on ranks, so heavy tails don’t fool it.
  • ClickBack to our islands. Where would four chains start? Stan starts every parameter at a random value between minus two and two, on the unconstrained scale: that’s the shaded box. These ticks are the actual starts, all four in the gap between the islands. A common explanation is that Stan starts chains out in the far corners. It doesn’t, and that box only counts as spread out if your posterior is narrower than it: one more reason to keep parameters on a sensible scale. And nothing decides which island each chain falls into.
  • One shortcut to avoid while we’re here: starting every chain at the optimiser’s answer to save time. Identical starts can’t disagree, so you throw away exactly the comparison R-hat relies on. And as we saw at the start, the mode isn’t where the mass is anyway.
  • ClickHere’s what happened. Same posterior, same settings, four chains: two went left, two went right. R-hat jumps from a reassuring 1.00 to 1.73. Don’t wait for numbers that dramatic, though. The modern R-hat saturates, so 1.05 is already a loud alarm.
  • PauseA question: how many chains do you need to catch this reliably? (Let them guess.)
  • ClickIf each chain picks an island at random, one chain hides the problem every time. Two chains hide it half the time. Four, one time in eight. Eight, under one percent. It’s odds, not a guarantee. Four chains on four cores take about as long as one, so four is a sensible minimum, not a magic number.
  • One more common explanation to correct: a high R-hat doesn’t automatically mean rewrite the model. Sometimes the chains are just too short. If it stays high when you run longer, as it would here, then it’s the model or the geometry.
  • R-hat tells us the chains agree. It doesn’t tell us how much information we’ve got. That’s ESS.
  • If asked“Should I set initial values myself?” Rarely. Rescale first; hand-set starts hide a scaling problem. If you do set them, make them different for each chain, or R-hat has nothing to compare.
  • If asked“R-hat is 1.02. Can I ignore it?” Not for final results. Run longer first; if it doesn’t come down, look at the model. For a quick exploratory fit, note it and move on.
  • If asked“Is this the same R-hat as Stan’s?” Yes: rank-normalised split-R-hat from Vehtari et al., 2021, computed live here and checked against ArviZ on the same draws. The islands on the right are a real NUTS run from the four starts shown.

    Sticky chains are worth far fewer draws than you ran

    Stickiness
    4,000 draws are worth–effective draws (bulk-ESS)

    Bulk-ESS : the centre (means, medians).

    Tail-ESS : the 5% and 95% quantiles, i.e. your interval endpoints.

    R-hat < 1.01 for every parameter Bulk- and tail-ESS > 100 per chain (400 with four) No divergences

    Passing these tells you the draws are trustworthy. How many digits you can report is a separate question.

    FTN
    ESS=N1+2∑t≥1ρt\text{ESS} = \dfrac{N}{1 + 2\sum_{t \ge 1} \rho_t}ESS=1+2∑t≥1​ρt​N​

    N draws, ρt the autocorrelation at lag t; the sum stops where the autocorrelations fade into noise.

  • About 2 minutes
  • Draws from a chain aren’t independent. Each step starts where the last one ended. ESS, the effective sample size, asks how many independent draws they’re actually worth.
  • Click through the stickiness buttonsIndependent draws are worth what you ran. As the chain gets stickier, the worth drops. Here, 4,000 sticky draws are worth about 200.
  • Under the hood, the software adds up these autocorrelation bars until they fade into noise. The dashed line is where it stops.
  • Stan reports two versions. Bulk-ESS is about the centre: means and medians. Tail-ESS is about the 5 and 95 percent points, the interval endpoints we put in every report. In real models the tail is often the weaker of the two.
  • Point at the checklistSo that’s three checks to pass before you trust any fit: R-hat under 1.01, bulk- and tail-ESS over 100 per chain, and no divergences.
  • Passing those tells you the draws are trustworthy. It doesn’t tell you how many digits to report. That’s the last check.
  • If asked“Why 100 per chain?” Below that, the R-hat and ESS estimates themselves become unreliable. It’s a floor, not a target.
  • If asked“How can ESS be bigger than the number of draws?” HMC draws can be negatively correlated, which is even better than independent. A good sign, not a bug.
  • If asked“For every parameter?” Yes, automatically, and the worst one counts. In an MMM that’s usually one of the hierarchical scale parameters.
  • If asked“Is this how Stan computes it?” Yes: bulk- and tail-ESS as in Stan and ArviZ (Vehtari et al., 2021), computed live here and checked against ArviZ on the same draws.

    Endpoints cost more (ESS 400)

    Tails are rare, so their estimates are noisier: that’s tail-ESS.

    Precision is expensive: half the noise costs 4× the draws; one more digit costs 100×.

    ✓ R-hat < 1.01✓ bulk- and tail-ESS > 100 per chain✓ no divergences✓ report digits to the MCSE
    FTN
    MCSE(mean)=posterior SDESS\text{MCSE}(\text{mean}) = \dfrac{\text{posterior SD}}{\sqrt{\text{ESS}}}MCSE(mean)=ESS​posterior SD​

    So MCSE ∝ 1/√ESS: half the noise takes 4× the effective draws.

  • About 2½ minutes · four clicks
  • Same model, same data, and nothing changed but the random seed. Twenty runs, twenty slightly different answers. That wobble isn’t uncertainty about the temperature trend; it comes from the simulation itself. It has a name: the Monte Carlo standard error, or MCSE.
  • Click through ESS 100 to 6,400It shrinks in proportion to one over the square root of ESS: four times the effective draws, half the wobble. And the shaded band, plus or minus two MCSE, really does capture where the reruns land.
  • ClickSo: the software prints 2.146924. How many decimals would you print? (Let them answer.)
  • ClickWith an MCSE around 0.05, the second decimal is already noise: rerun and it changes. Writing 2.146 in a table claims a precision the simulation never earned. The honest number is 2.1. And if a decision really needs 2.15, you don’t type it, you buy it: run longer until the MCSE supports it.
  • ClickTwo more things. The interval endpoints are the noisiest numbers we report, here about three times the MCSE of the mean, because the tails are rare. And precision is expensive: halving the noise costs four times the effective draws, and one more digit costs a hundred times as many. So decide what precision the decision needs, and size the run for that. While you’re still building a model, fit fast and fail fast; a few hundred iterations is plenty to find bugs.
  • For our ROI tables, that means: if two channels’ ROIs differ by less than their MCSEs, the simulation can’t rank them, however many decimals we show.
  • Which brings me to what I think this means for the tool we build.
  • If asked“Isn’t this tiny next to the posterior uncertainty?” Usually, yes: here 0.05 against a posterior standard deviation of 0.5. MCSE decides how many digits to print, not how certain we are. Both belong in the report.
  • If asked“Should I always run 100,000 iterations?” Only if the decision needs it. ESS ≈ (posterior SD ÷ target MCSE)² tells you how many.
  • If asked“Where do I find MCSE?” It’s a column in az.summary and in Stan’s summary; quantile MCSE comes from az.mcse.
  • If asked“Is this the book’s data?” No: simulated trend data in the spirit of the chapter’s temperature example. The reruns are real NUTS runs, four chains each, with MCSEs from ArviZ.
    • Bayesian Workflow · Chapter 1111

    Our tool should make the safe path the default

    Before anyone trusts a fit

    R-hat < 1.01

    Bulk- and tail-ESS > 100 per chain

    No divergences

    Digits reported to the MCSE

    What we build in

    1. Four chains by default
    2. Inputs auto-scaled; chains never started at the MAP
    3. R-hat and ESS as gates: a failed check stops the run
    4. MCSE shown next to every ROI, digits rounded to it

    What we said you’d know

    What can’t a single chain tell you?
    Whether it’s complete. Only other chains show what it missed.
    What do R-hat, ESS and MCSE test?
    Do chains agree; how much information; how precise each number is.
    How many digits may you report?
    Only those larger than the MCSE.

    Further reading: chapter 11 on replicability and simulation-based calibration (SBC).

  • About 1 minute, then questions
  • Here’s the whole talk on one slide. On the left, the four checks a fit should pass before anyone looks at an ROI.
  • On the right, what this means for us. We don’t fit the models ourselves, but every modeller who does goes through our tool, so its defaults decide what happens. The aim is to make the safe path the default, so nobody has to remember any of this.
  • Four chains by default; on four cores they cost about the same wall-clock time as one. Scale inputs automatically, and never start chains at the MAP. Make R-hat and ESS gates, so a failed check stops the run instead of printing a warning nobody reads. And show MCSE next to every ROI, and round to it, so the digits a modeller copies into a deck are digits they’ve earned.
  • Point at the bandAnd the promise from the start. A single chain can’t tell you whether it’s complete. R-hat tests whether chains agree, ESS how much information you have, and MCSE how precise each number is. And you don’t report digits smaller than the MCSE.
  • We didn’t get to the chapter’s material on replicability and simulation-based calibration; that’s the further reading. Thank you. Questions?
  • If asked“Why does scaling the inputs matter so much?” Stan’s random starts assume parameters of order one. Leave spend in raw kroner and they make the model compute exp() of something huge, so the sampler can’t even start: in a Poisson MMM I tried, all 100 default starts failed. With standardised spend the same model starts first time, and warm-up is faster too.
  • If asked“Doesn’t the tool scale inputs already?” Mostly. It bites on new model types and on the unscaled pieces: raw-unit intercepts, adstock or saturation priors far from order one. When a modeller reports Stan rejecting initial values, that’s the symptom.
  • If asked“Won’t hard gates frustrate the modellers?” Only when something’s wrong, which is the point. Keep an explicit, logged override for quick exploratory fits, so a failed check can never slip into a client result silently.
  • If asked“Why never start at the MAP?” Identical starts can’t disagree, so R-hat loses its power, and the MAP isn’t in the typical set anyway. It saves a little warm-up and costs you the check.
